Bug_Title: Inappropriate "Collection" calls should not be made
Bug_Details:
The java.util.Collection type and its subtypes provide methods to access and modify collections such as Collection.remove(Object
o) and Collection.contains(Object o) . Some of these methods accept arguments of type java.lang.Object and will
compare said argument with objects already in the collection.
If the actual type of the argument is unrelated to the type of object contained in the collection, these methods will always return false , null , or -1 . This behavior is most likely unintended and can be indicative of a design issue.
This rule raises an issue when the type of the argument provided to one of the following methods is unrelated to the type used for the collection
declaration:
Collection.remove(Object o) Collection.removeAll(Collection<?>) Collection.contains(Object o) List.indexOf(Object o) List.lastIndexOf(Object o) Map.containsKey(Object key) Map.containsValue(Object value) Map.get(Object key) Map.getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue) Map.remove(Object key) Map.remove(Object key, Object value)
Collection.remove(Object o)
Collection.removeAll(Collection<?>)
Collection.contains(Object o)
List.indexOf(Object o)
List.lastIndexOf(Object o)
Map.containsKey(Object key)
Map.containsValue(Object value)
Map.get(Object key)
Map.getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue)
Map.remove(Object key)
Map.remove(Object key, Object value)
Bug_Explanation: The code demonstrates inappropriate Collection calls by using argument types in collection methods that are unrelated to the types contained in the collections. This leads to always returning false or null. For instance, using a String to check presence in a List of Integers, or checking a String key in a Map with Integer keys.
Trigger_Explanation: The JUnit test cases trigger the bug by passing arguments to collection methods that have unrelated types to the collection's stored types, consistently leading to false, null, or -1 results, which are unintended.
